questions.question: For losses with CDFs $F_X,F_Y$, assume $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y$, so $F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)$ at every real $t$. Which strict-tail relation is guaranteed for every such law pair and threshold by taking complements?
options: $\mathbb{P}(X>t)\ge\mathbb{P}(Y>t)$.
$\mathbb{P}(X\ge t)=1-F_X(t)$.
$\mathbb{P}(X>t)=F_X(t)$.
$\mathbb{P}(X>t)\le\mathbb{P}(Y>t)$.

questions.question: An insurer knows the two marginal loss CDFs but no joint distribution of X and Y. Can it decide stochastic order from those CDFs alone?
options: Yes; compare the two CDFs at every real threshold.
No; it must first establish independence of X and Y.
No; it must first observe both losses in the same outcome.
Yes; the larger maximum possible loss alone decides the order.

questions.question: Losses X,Y have finite equal means and satisfy $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y$. What follows about their marginal distributions?
options: Only their zero-loss probabilities must agree.
Y must have strictly more tail probability somewhere.
They are identical.
X and Y must be independent.

questions.question: To establish $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y$ using bounded increasing functions h, what is required of their expectations?
options: The inequality for one selected such h is sufficient.
$\mathbb{E}[h(X)]\le\mathbb{E}[h(Y)]$ for every such h.
The inequality only for constant h is sufficient.
The inequality for one h must be strict.

questions.question: Losses satisfy $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y$. A decision maker has fixed initial wealth $w$ and increasing utility $u$, with both expected utilities finite. Which final-wealth utility comparison is guaranteed for every such law pair and utility?
options: $\mathbb{E}[u(w-X)]\ge\mathbb{E}[u(w-Y)]$.
$\mathbb{E}[u(w-X)]\le\mathbb{E}[u(w-Y)]$.
$\mathbb{E}[u(w-X)]=\mathbb{E}[u(w-Y)]$ for every u.
The comparison needs u to be strictly concave.

questions.question: A loss X is zero with probability 0.3 and one with probability 0.7. To test the defining strict-tail inequality at threshold 1, what value is used for the X side?
options: The left limit of the CDF,0.3.

questions.question: X is 0 or 4 equally likely, while Y is 1 or 5 equally likely. For the increasing cap $h(z)=\min(z,3)$ on non-negative losses, compare their expected transformed losses.
options: They are 2 and 3, respectively.
They are 3 and 3, respectively.
They are 1.5 and 2, respectively.
They are 2 and 1.5, respectively.

questions.question: For losses X,Y,Z, suppose $F_X(t)\ge F_Y(t)$ and $F_Y(t)\ge F_Z(t)$ for every real t. What makes $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Z$ follow?
options: The three losses must be independent.
The two inequalities chain at each identical threshold.
The intermediate CDF can be compared at a different threshold.
The two comparisons force all three laws to coincide.

questions.question: Bounded losses satisfy $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y$ and both lie in[0,w], where w is a fixed wealth amount. What stochastic order holds for their remaining wealth w-X,w-Y?
options: $w-X\le_{\mathrm{st}}w-Y$.
Both directions always hold.
Neither direction can hold after subtraction.
$w-Y\le_{\mathrm{st}}w-X$.

questions.question: Non-negative losses have strict tails $\mathbb{P}(X>t)=\mathrm{e}^{-2t}$ and $\mathbb{P}(Y>t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t}$ for $t\ge0$. Which stochastic comparison follows?
options: The faster-decaying X tail makes Y stochastically smaller.
The identical limiting tails imply identical loss laws.
Different exponential rates prevent any stochastic comparison.
The faster-decaying X tail makes X stochastically smaller.

questions.question: The joint outcomes (X,Y)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1) have probabilities 0.48,0.32,0.12,0.08. Their marginal positive-loss probabilities are 0.2 and 0.4. An analyst infers $X\le Y$ almost surely from their stochastic order. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The inference fails: the outcome (1,0) has probability 0.12.
The inference holds: ordered marginal laws force pointwise order.
The inference fails: the outcome (1,1) has probability 0.08.
The inference holds: all X-positive outcomes also have Y positive.

questions.question: X is certainly 2. Y is 0 or 6 equally likely, so its mean 3 exceeds X’s mean 2. Do these laws nevertheless fail both stochastic directions?
options: No; the larger mean guarantees X is stochastically smaller.
No; the larger maximum guarantees X is stochastically smaller.
Yes; their CDF inequalities have opposite directions at 1 and 3.
Yes; any different supports preclude stochastic order.

questions.question: X is certainly 1 and Y certainly 2, so X is stochastically no larger than Y. Compare their probabilities of falling in the interval(0.5,1.5]. Does this interval probability inherit the same direction?
options: Yes; the probabilities are 0 and 1, as required by order.
No; they are 1 and 0, and the interval indicator decreases above 1.5.
Yes; both probabilities equal 1 because both losses exceed 0.5.
No; this reversal proves the original stochastic comparison was wrong.

questions.question: X is 0 or 2 equally likely and Y is certainly 1. A check uses only thresholds 0 and 2 and finds F_X at least F_Y there. Does that sparse check prove X is stochastically no larger than Y?
options: Yes; the endpoints of their combined support suffice here.
Yes; equality of the two means supplies the missing inequalities.
No; at threshold 2 the CDF values are 1/2 and 1.
No; at threshold 1 the CDF values are 1/2 and 1.

questions.question: On support 0,1,2, X has probabilities $(0.5,0.3,0.2)$ and Y has $(0.2,0.4,0.4)$. Which full stochastic comparison follows?
options: The larger Y CDF establishes only the Y-to-X stochastic direction.
The two complete CDFs agree at every threshold.
The larger X CDF establishes only the X-to-Y stochastic direction.
The cumulative comparisons reverse inside the support.

questions.question: Non-negative losses satisfy $\min(X,1)\le_{\mathrm{st}}\min(Y,1)$, where $z\mapsto\min(z,1)$ is increasing. Does it follow that $X\le_{\mathrm{st}}Y$?
options: No; $X=3$ and $Y=2$ surely both cap to $1$.
Yes; increasing maps preserve stochastic order in both directions.
Yes; the cap is increasing, so it can be undone on the CDFs.
No; the cap is decreasing above $1$, so the order reverses there.

questions.question: X is uniform on $[0,2]$ and Y uniform on $[1,3]$. Their CDFs are linear from 0 to 1 on those intervals and constant outside. Which conclusion follows from checking the overlap $[1,2]$ and both nonoverlap regions?
options: Their overlapping supports prevent a stochastic comparison.
The one-unit shift makes Y the stochastically larger loss.
The one-unit shift makes X the stochastically larger loss.
Equal interval lengths make their full CDFs identical.
